strengths: Clear and rigorous technical contribution: Rank-GRPO addresses genuine misalignment in GRPO for rank-structured outputs, with elegant gradient analysis (Eq. 4-7) demonstrating non-causal credit assignment and importance ratio mismatch
Well-motivated problem with practical relevance: Identifies concrete challenges (catalog unawareness, format violations, tail degradation) in applying LLMs to conversational recommendation
Thoughtful two-stage framework: Remap-Reflect-Adjust pipeline creatively addresses the lack of high-quality in-catalog ranking data using teacher LLM distillation
Strong empirical results: Small models trained with ConvRec-R1 match/exceed GPT-4o and CRAG on REDDIT-V2, with demonstrable improvements especially at tail positions
Comprehensive experimental analysis: Multiple backbones (0.5B, 1B, 3B), on-policy/off-policy settings, training dynamics visualization, and qualitative examples
Excellent reproducibility: Promises to release code, dataset, trained checkpoints, with thorough implementation details (Appendix C)
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: Single dataset (REDDIT-V2) and single domain (movies) prevent generalizability claims; no evaluation on e-commerce, books, or other domains despite claiming broad applicability to rank-structured tasks

Missing critical comparison: RecLLM-R1 (Xie et al., 2025), the most directly related concurrent work on GRPO-based CRS, is mentioned but never experimentally compared despite targeting the same problem on the same dataset

Insufficient algorithmic justification: Reward shaping choices (Eq. 8-9) lack rigor—why is Γ = ∞ optimal? Penalties for incomplete/overflow items (ϵu, ϵo) appear ad-hoc; hyperparameters (λ, γ, λw, λb) not ablated

Overlooked practical concerns: Teacher LLM cost (multiple GPT-4o API calls for Remap-Reflect-Adjust) never discussed; figure 6 shows both methods drift from catalog during RL with insufficient investigation of solutions
Missing ablation studies: No isolated evaluation of Remap-Reflect-Adjust components; sensitivity to key hyperparameters (especially Γ) not analyzed
Unexplored cost-efficiency tradeoffs: Dependence on teacher LLM for training data generation undermines efficiency advantages claimed for small models; actual deployment cost not addressed

Inconsistent experimental setup: Requiring title+release year makes comparison with prior work difficult; exact-match parsing success rates not reported; one-month validation-test gap may mask distribution shift
Statistical rigor gaps: Error bars provided but no hypothesis tests; some improvements (Recall@5: 0.005-0.015) may be within error margins; no significance thresholds discussed

strengths: Clear problem motivation with three identified limitations of LLM-based CRS
Principled gradient analysis (Equations 4 vs. 7) demonstrating misalignment of vanilla GRPO for rank-structured outputs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple backbones (0.5B, 1B, 3B) and both on-policy/off-policy settings
Practical impact: small LLMs match/exceed GPT-4o performance with proper training
Extensive implementation details and reproducibility commitment
Systematic two-stage approach addressing catalog grounding and ranking quality sequentially
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Stage 1 combines existing techniques (similarity matching, LLM-as-judge, parametric bias learning) with primarily engineering contributions
Rank-GRPO is an incremental adaptation of GRPO (rank-level importance ratio, geometric mean normalization) rather than a fundamental algorithmic advance
Single-dataset evaluation (REDDIT-V2 only) limits generalization claims; no evidence of transfer to other domains or recommendation types
Modest absolute improvements: 8-10% relative gains in key metrics, which may not justify the added complexity
Critical missing ablations: no ablation of Remap-Reflect-Adjust components, geometric mean vs. alternatives, or hyperparameter Γ values beyond Γ = ∞
No theoretical justification for design choices: geometric mean normalization, DCG@k:N reward formulation, or rank-wise advantage approximation
Experimental design concerns: GRPO and Rank-GRPO use different clip ranges (0.2-0.26 vs. 0.06-0.08); unclear if both methods equally tuned
No comparison with concurrent work (RecLLM-R1, Rec-R1) on identical benchmarks despite mentioning them in related work
Missing user studies: all evaluation relies on automatic metrics; real user preferences unknown
Presentation density: paper tries to cover distillation pipeline + RL algorithm + extensive experiments, making core contributions less clear

strengths: Clear problem diagnosis with gradient analysis demonstrating fundamental misalignment of GRPO for ranking tasks (Eq. 4-5, 16)
Principled algorithmic contribution: Rank-GRPO elegantly identifies rank as the natural action unit for credit assignment and importance weighting
Strong empirical results across multiple model sizes (0.5B, 1B, 3B), demonstrating that small open-source LLMs can match/exceed GPT-4o performance
Comprehensive experiments with both on-policy and off-policy settings; clear improvements particularly on tail positions where vanilla GRPO degrades
Practical significance: single forward pass vs. CRAG's 5-7 API calls per recommendation; code and datasets promised for release
Well-designed Remap-Reflect-Adjust pipeline for generating catalog-grounded training data without manual annotation
Detailed presentation with full gradient derivations, implementation details, and qualitative examples supporting interpretability
weaknesses: Evaluation limited to single domain (movie recommendation on REDDIT-V2); claims of broad applicability to rank-structured tasks lack empirical support across domains (books, products, music, etc.)
Missing direct comparison with concurrent related work Rec-R1 (Lin et al., 2025) and RecLLM-R1 (Xie et al., 2025), which address similar problems and are essential for positioning novelty
Remap-Reflect-Adjust pipeline is complex with multiple hyperparameters (λ=1, γ=0.5, etc.) that appear somewhat arbitrary; lacks systematic ablation of individual component contributions
Catalog drift during RL training (Figure 6) occurs for both GRPO and Rank-GRPO (~87% in-catalog by end); practical deployment concern not adequately addressed
Off-policy stability issues: Llama-3.2-1B requires special learning rate schedule to prevent divergence; suggests brittleness for certain model sizes
Reward masking design (Eq. 8-9) and exponential decay with Γ=∞ lack strong theoretical justification despite being empirically motivated
Remap-Reflect-Adjust pipeline is movie-specific (RAG on IMDb/Wikipedia, metadata format); transferability to other domains (products, books) questionable but claimed as generalizable
Statistical significance concerns: some improvements marginal relative to error bars; off-policy results within error ranges for certain comparisons
Missing critical analysis: no discussion of failure modes, when method underperforms, or guidelines for practitioners on when to apply approach

strengths: Well-identified problem in applying GRPO to ranking tasks with clear gradient analysis demonstrating misalignment between sequence-level rewards and token-level updates
Practical two-stage framework with well-designed Remap-Reflect-Adjust pipeline that cleverly leverages teacher LLM knowledge without human annotations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model sizes (0.5B, 1B, 3B), datasets (REDDIT-V2, REDIAL), and training settings (on-policy and off-policy)
Strong empirical results with Llama-3.2-3B variant surpassing GPT-4o and CRAG, showing practical value for smaller models
Detailed ablation studies and training dynamics analysis providing interpretable insights into method behavior
Reproducibility commitment with code, datasets, and trained checkpoints to be released
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of core components: Remap-Reflect-Adjust pipeline combines existing techniques (semantic similarity, LLM-as-judge, bias learning) heuristically without principled justification; Rank-GRPO itself is a reasonable but incremental algorithmic adaptation

Rank-GRPO lacks theoretical grounding: reward decomposition (Eq. 8-9) is intuitive but arbitrary; geometric mean for importance weighting lacks principled justification; no convergence analysis or optimality guarantees

Narrow evaluation scope: movies only across all datasets; generalization to other domains (e-commerce, video) with different item representations unclear; evaluation limited to ranking metrics without diversity/novelty metrics or human evaluation

Catalog drift problem inadequately addressed: Figure 6 shows in-catalog hit ratio degrades from ~100% to 85-95% during RL training, contradicting SFT grounding; no effective mitigation strategy proposed
Off-policy training exhibits significant performance degradation (5-10% worse metrics, Table 4) limiting practical utility for efficient trajectory reuse; underlying causes not thoroughly analyzed

Incomplete baseline comparisons: no direct comparison with concurrent RecLLM-R1; DPO baselines adapted indirectly via BIGRec potentially unfair; limited engagement with other RL-based recommendation methods

Teacher LLM dependency underexplored: SFT quality strongly depends on teacher model; no analysis of performance with weaker teachers; Reflect step requires multiple teacher calls increasing deployment cost

Extensive hyperparameter tuning with limited sensitivity analysis: Remap-Reflect-Adjust introduces λ, γ, w, b; reward shaping adds Γ, ϵo, ϵu; only ϵo sensitivity provided (Fig. 10); concern about dataset-specific tuning

Evaluation methodology limitations: binary relevance oversimplifies preferences; standard errors substantial (~0.002-0.0035); no statistical significance testing; lack of human evaluation on recommendation quality aspects
Missing computational cost analysis: Remap-Reflect-Adjust requires multiple teacher LLM calls; no wall-clock time comparisons; deployment efficiency vs baselines unknown

strengths: Clear identification of practical limitations in applying LLMs to CRS with well-motivated solutions
Principled gradient analysis clearly demonstrating token/sequence-level misalignment in GRPO for ranking tasks
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model sizes, on/off-policy settings, and ablation studies
Strong empirical results competitive with GPT-4o on REDDIT-V2
Extensive implementation details and reproducibility commitment
weaknesses: Limited and incremental novelty: Rank-GRPO is a straightforward granularity shift from tokens/sequences to ranks; RRA pipeline is standard engineering combining similarity matching, LLM-as-judge, and bias correction
Severely limited scope: All experiments restricted to movie recommendation (REDDIT-V2 and REDIAL); claims of applicability to 'rank-structured outputs' broadly are unsupported
Questionable experimental setup: Critical dependency on expensive proprietary models (GPT-4o) for SFT data generation; arbitrary design choices (25% data fraction, hyperparameters) lack justification

Weak baseline comparisons: Limited GRPO/GSPO analysis; DPO variants in Appendix D.3 achieve competitive results, undermining claimed advantages; unfair CRAG comparison (different approach + model size conflation)

Technical concerns: DCG@k:N reward decomposition is artificial; Γ=∞ in Eq. 9 lacks theoretical justification; geometric mean choice unexplored; approximation quality of rank-wise advantage estimation not analyzed
Off-policy performance significantly degrades (Table 4), suggesting method may not be robust for trajectory reuse in practical settings
Catalog drift problem (Figure 6) undermines key motivation despite claims of improvement

Overclaimed contributions: 'Principled' and 'fundamental resolution' language overstates what is domain-specific, empirical engineering; gradient analysis critique of GRPO is valid but the proposed fix still applies token-level gradients grouped by rank

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with clear articulation of three key challenges (catalog grounding, format adherence, tail degradation) in LLM-based recommendations
Excellent technical analysis with principled gradient derivations (Eq. 4-5) clearly demonstrating GRPO's mismatch with ranking tasks
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple scales (0.5B-3B), on/off-policy settings, with clear training dynamics visualizations showing rank-wise improvements
Practical impact: small open-source models (3B) match/exceed GPT-4o performance, with significant implications for cost and latency
Thorough reproducibility: code and datasets released, detailed hyperparameters, comprehensive appendices with ablations and sensitivity analyses
Effective Remap-Reflect-Adjust pipeline with clear intuition and concrete examples demonstrating each step's contribution
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Rank-GRPO is a relatively straightforward extension of GRPO once the problem is identified; Remap-Reflect-Adjust is primarily engineering combining existing techniques
Single domain evaluation: experiments only on movie recommendation (REDDIT-V2, REDIAL); no evaluation on e-commerce, books, music, or other domains despite generalization claims

Under-justified design choices: exponential decay with Γ=∞ performs best but is extreme and seemingly contradicts Eq. (5) motivation for causal downstream effects; limited ablation of normalization schemes (geometric vs. arithmetic mean)
Unresolved catalog drift issue: Figure 6 shows both GRPO and Rank-GRPO drift from ~100% to ~95% in-catalog rate; while Rank-GRPO drifts slower, root causes and solutions are not addressed

Significant off-policy performance gap: Table 4 shows non-trivial NDCG drops (e.g., 0.1079→0.1025 for 0.5B model); limits practical efficiency gains from trajectory reuse and suggests rank-level importance weighting still struggles with variance
Limited analysis of failure modes: qualitative examples show only successes; no discussion of when/why Rank-GRPO underperforms or what types of conversations are hard
Teacher model dependency not analyzed: SFT critically depends on powerful teachers (GPT-4o/Claude); sensitivity to weaker teachers and quality thresholds missing
Scale limitations: models capped at 3B; 7B results only on smaller REDIAL dataset; unclear how approach scales to modern 7B+ models
